slides.title: Hardware, Virtualization, and Cloud Vulnerabilities
points: Infrastructure vulnerabilities can exist in firmware, end-of-life hardware, virtual machines, shared resources, cloud configurations, and upstream providers.
Security+ Objective 2.3: explain various types of vulnerabilities.

slides.title: Firmware
slides.teach: Low-level software embedded in hardware that can contain vulnerabilities or malicious code.

course.learn: Low-level software embedded in hardware that can contain vulnerabilities or malicious code.

breakdown.explanation: Firmware is the software that helps hardware operate.

course.why: Firmware vulnerabilities can persist below the operating system and may be difficult to detect or patch.
course.example: A router firmware flaw allows remote compromise.
course.check_q: Which vulnerability category involves software embedded in hardware?

slides.title: End-of-life
slides.teach: Hardware or software that has reached the end of vendor support and may no longer receive security fixes.

course.learn: Hardware or software that has reached the end of vendor support and may no longer receive security fixes.

breakdown.explanation: The vendor has stopped supporting it.

course.why: New vulnerabilities may remain permanently unpatched.
course.example: An appliance remains in production after the vendor ends security updates.
course.check_q: Which category means vendor support has ended?

slides.title: Legacy
slides.teach: Older technology still in use even though newer alternatives exist.

course.learn: Older technology still in use even though newer alternatives exist.

breakdown.explanation: It is old, but not necessarily unsupported.

course.why: Legacy technology may have compatibility limitations, weaker security designs, or operational dependence.
course.example: A business application still depends on an old protocol.
course.check_q: Which term describes outdated technology still in use?

slides.title: Virtual Machine (VM) Escape
slides.teach: A vulnerability that allows code in a guest VM to break isolation and interact with the host or other VMs.

course.learn: A vulnerability that allows code in a guest VM to break isolation and interact with the host or other VMs.

breakdown.explanation: The guest escapes its virtual boundary.

course.why: VM escape defeats virtualization isolation and can expose other workloads or the host.
course.example: Malicious code inside a guest compromises the hypervisor.
course.check_q: Which vulnerability lets a guest VM break isolation?

slides.title: Resource Reuse
slides.teach: Risk created when reused memory, storage, or other resources expose residual data from a previous user or process.

course.learn: Risk created when reused memory, storage, or other resources expose residual data from a previous user or process.

breakdown.explanation: Old data remains after the resource is reassigned.

course.why: Residual data can leak across users, processes, or tenants.
course.example: A newly allocated memory region contains another tenant's data.
course.exam: Old data in reused resource → RESOURCE REUSE.
course.check_q: Which vulnerability involves residual data in reused resources?

slides.title: Cloud-specific
slides.teach: Vulnerabilities unique or especially relevant to cloud environments, often involving identity, APIs, configuration, tenancy, or shared responsibility.

course.learn: Vulnerabilities unique or especially relevant to cloud environments, often involving identity, APIs, configuration, tenancy, or shared responsibility.

breakdown.explanation: The weakness comes from cloud architecture, permissions, or configuration.
Public storage bucket, Overprivileged cloud role

course.why: Cloud services expose unique control planes and shared-responsibility boundaries.
course.example: A cloud bucket is accidentally configured for public access.
course.check_q: Which category fits a public cloud bucket caused by incorrect cloud permissions?

slides.title: Service Provider
slides.teach: A provider whose compromise or weakness can affect customers relying on its hosted or managed service.

course.learn: A provider whose compromise or weakness can affect customers relying on its hosted or managed service.

breakdown.explanation: A trusted service dependency introduces upstream risk.
Cloud service provider, Managed SaaS provider

course.why: Customers inherit some risk from the service provider's controls and security posture.
course.example: A SaaS provider compromise exposes customer data.
course.exam: Trusted service provider weakness → SERVICE PROVIDER.
course.check_q: Which supply-chain category describes a compromised hosted service provider?

slides.title: Hardware Provider
slides.teach: A supplier of physical devices or components whose products can introduce security weaknesses.

course.learn: A supplier of physical devices or components whose products can introduce security weaknesses.

breakdown.explanation: The upstream risk comes from hardware or components.

course.why: Compromised or defective hardware can enter the environment before deployment.
course.example: A malicious component is introduced during hardware manufacturing.
course.check_q: Which provider category relates to compromised hardware components?

slides.title: Software Provider
slides.teach: A supplier of applications, libraries, or updates whose compromise can affect downstream customers.

course.learn: A supplier of applications, libraries, or updates whose compromise can affect downstream customers.

breakdown.explanation: The upstream risk comes from software the organization trusts.

course.why: A compromised software provider can distribute malicious code broadly.
course.example: A trusted library maintainer's package is compromised.
course.check_q: Which provider category relates to compromised applications or libraries?

blocks.title: Infrastructure vulnerability exam shortcuts
items: Legacy means outdated technology remains in operation; it does not automatically mean vendor support has ended.
Example: A business application still depends on an old protocol.
End-of-life means the vendor has stopped supporting the product.
Example: An appliance remains in production after security updates stop.
A virtual machine breaks the isolation boundary.
Example: Malicious code in a guest compromises the hypervisor or host.
Old data appears in reused resource → RESOURCE REUSE
The issue is leftover information that was not cleared before reuse.
Example: Newly allocated memory contains another tenant's data.
The weakness arises from cloud configuration, identity, tenancy, APIs, or shared-responsibility mistakes.
Example: A storage bucket is accidentally public.
The risk originates from a service, hardware, or software provider that the organization trusts.
Example: A software provider distributes a compromised package.
blocks.example: Memory: Legacy = old · EOL = unsupported · VM escape = isolation failure · Resource reuse = leftover data.

questions.q: An appliance is still running, but its vendor stopped releasing security updates two years ago. Which vulnerability category best fits?
questions.explanation: The key clue is that vendor support and security updates have ended.

questions.q: An old application still uses an outdated protocol, but the vendor still provides support. Which category best fits?
questions.explanation: Legacy means old technology still in use; support may or may not have ended.

questions.q: Malicious code inside a guest virtual machine breaks out and interacts with the host. Which vulnerability is this?
A newly allocated memory region contains data left by a previous tenant. Which vulnerability is this?
questions.explanation: Residual data was not cleared before the resource was reused.

questions.q: A cloud storage bucket is made public because of an incorrect access setting. Which category best fits?
questions.explanation: The weakness comes from cloud configuration and access control.

questions.q: A router contains a vulnerability in its embedded low-level operating code. Which category best fits?
questions.explanation: The flaw exists in embedded firmware.

questions.q: A compromised software package maintainer distributes malicious code to organizations that depend on the package. Which provider category is most relevant?
questions.explanation: The upstream risk originates from a software provider.
